# Cadence — task list

The running record of work: open, in progress, done, cancelled. Started 2026-08-16.

**Format.** One line per item: `- [id] Title — note`. Ids are stable and never reused, so a
cancelled or done item can still be referenced later. Done items keep their commit sha, because the
commit message is where the *reasoning* lives; this file is only the index.

**Rule (set 2026-08-17).** *Every* request the user makes lands here the moment it is made, whether
or not work starts on it — under **In progress** if it is being worked now, otherwise under the
right Open section. An item moves to **Done** only when the code behind it is committed (or
otherwise verified), not when it is written.

**Target devices** (set 2026-08-16). Build and verify for these three only; anything that exists
solely to serve other hardware is dead weight and should be removed rather than maintained:

| Device | Points | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| iPhone 15 (base) | 393 × 852 | compact width, the only phone shape that matters |
| iPad Pro 11" | 834 × 1210 portrait · 1210 × 834 landscape | pane = window − 188pt sidebar → **646** portrait, **1022** landscape |
| MacBook Pro 14" | 1512 × 982 | the macOS surface |

Both iPad panes matter to Today's layout: 646pt portrait falls **below**
`CadenceTodayLayoutSupport.twoPaneMinimumWidth` (761), so portrait is one column and landscape is
two. The three-pane floor of 1022pt that this note used to cite is gone with the layout itself
(T-06).

---

- [T-2077] **PARTIALLY CLOSED 2026-10-05 (agent `cutwrites`, increment 3 — stop the writes) — every path that wrote a `Goal`, a `Habit`, a `HabitCompletion` or a `GoalListLink` **without a user asking** is gone, and so is the MCP write surface; the in-app editor sheets are NOT, and are [[T-2079]].** The owner retired habits and goals before the next TestFlight build and chose the depth explicitly: *"remove UI and stop writing, keep the schema"* — the app never creates or updates a habit/goal record again, the old records sit inert in iCloud, and the decision stays reversible. `Habit`, `HabitCompletion`, `HabitInsights`, `Goal`, `GoalContributionSummary`, `GoalListLink` and `GoalPresentation` all stay; nothing in this increment deletes, rewrites or migrates an existing row. Production held 2 habits, 7 habit completions and 5 goals when it was filed. `cutnav` took navigation and `cutwidgets` the widgets in the same ticket.
  **1. The MCP write surface: the tools are GONE, not refusing.** `create_goal` and `create_habit` are removed from `CadenceMCPToolDefinitions.writeToolNames`, from `allTools`, from the router, and `createGoal`/`createHabit` with their options structs, audit entries, five error cases and six private validators are removed from `CadenceWriteService` (−14 KB of a 131 KB file). Disappearing beats refusing on the one argument a client can act on: `tools/list` is the only capability contract it can read, `tools(writesEnabled:)` already filters on exactly this set, and a tool that stays advertised and always errors costs a round trip to learn what the list could have said. A tool that silently answered OK and wrote nothing would be worse than either. `serverVersion` and the `initialize` handshake both go **0.13.0 → 0.14.0** — the first bump here that *removes* tools, which is why it is a minor and not a patch even though no response key moved. `list_goals`, `get_goal` and `list_habits` are untouched: this removes the ability to mint, not the ability to see. `arguments.intArray` and `arguments.double` went with them, because [[T-260]]'s rule — enforced by `everyArgumentParsingHelperIsCalledByTheRouter`, which caught them — is that an uncalled parsing helper is deleted rather than left one keystroke from the live ones.
  **2. `PursuitToGoalMigration` was a launch-time `Goal` constructor, and the flag was never what stopped it.** It ran from `PersistenceController.performStartupMaintenance` on every launch, and on a surviving `Pursuit` row it minted a `Goal`, inserted it, re-hung that pursuit's child goals and habits off it and saved — no user action anywhere. "The owner migrated years ago" was never enough: [[T-393]] made the pass content-aware *precisely because* `PersistenceController.init` applies a pending restore before it opens the container, so a store that already migrated can be replaced by a pre-merge backup and the pass re-probes and re-runs with the flag set. `runIfNeeded` now answers `.nothingToDo` and touches neither the store nor the flag; `migrate` and `hasSurvivingPursuits` are deleted. A surviving pursuit is now in exactly the position a goal is — present in the schema, present in CloudKit, read by nothing — so folding one into the other would move a row nobody can see into another row nobody can see. The pass is kept rather than deleted so [[T-1366]]'s `.pursuitMigration` stage and `CadenceFirstLaunchEmptyStoreTests`' derived pass set do not move.
  **3. Startup repair wrote a `Habit` and DELETED a `HabitCompletion`.** `repairOutOfRangeHabitReminders` (T-428 (filed only in a commit message, never in the ledger)) cleared `Habit.reminderMinuteOfDay` outside `0...1439`; `repairDuplicateHabitCompletions` ([[T-359]]) *deleted* check-in rows. Both on launch, unattended. Both are gone. Nothing is lost by stopping: the reminder value was already inert on both halves — `HabitNotificationPlanner.reminder(for:now:)` has refused an out-of-range minute since [[T-363]] — and the duplicate collapse was three things together, one writer, a read that collapses and this delete; the **read** (`HabitCompletion.collapsedCount(of:)`, a `max`) is untouched, so a duplicated day still reads as one. The delete was the only one of the three that could not be undone, and with every habit surface gone the owner cannot see a row disappear, let alone put it back. `duplicateHabitCompletionsRemoved` and `habitRemindersCleared` stay on `DataIntegrityRepairReport` and stay decoded — an earlier build's persisted report still carries the keys — and are simply never raised. **This also improves [[T-1088]]**: a split habit-day that was really worth 3 used to be flattened to 2 *permanently*; both rows now stay on disk and only the read reports 2, which is the only non-guessing answer to a question the archive carries no field to settle.
  **4. What was deliberately NOT removed, each with its reason.** (a) The context/area/project **merges'** re-pointing of `goal.context` / `habit.context` in `DataIntegrityRepairService`: it fires only when a duplicate `Context` already exists and is about to be deleted, and it moves a surviving goal or habit onto the canonical row instead of letting the delete nullify its filing — removing it would make this ticket *lose* data on the rows it exists to preserve. It writes a relationship to keep an existing row intact; it never creates one. (b) `CadenceArchiveImportService`, which restores `Goal`/`Habit`/`HabitCompletion`/`GoalListLink` rows from the owner's own backup: an import that refused them would make every backup silently lossy, which is the opposite of the reversibility this depth was chosen for. It is a deliberate user action, not a launch path. (c) `ModelContext.deleteContext`'s cascade in `CadenceListDeleteHelpers`, which still deletes a context's goals, habits, completions and goal links — that is the user destroying a context on purpose, it is announced by `CadenceListDeletionSummary`, and changing what a list delete *means* is a behaviour change rather than the removal of a write. **It is the one remaining path that can destroy one of these rows, and it is worth the owner knowing that.**
  **5. No task operation writes a goal.** Measured, because the brief suspected one: goal progress is **computed**, not stored — `GoalContributionSummary` is a plain `struct` built by `GoalContributionResolver` on read, not a `@Model` — so completing, rescheduling, duplicating or cancelling a task updates no `Goal` row. `AppTask.goal`, `CadenceTaskRecurrenceWorkflowSupport`'s `nextTask.goal = task.goal` and `CadenceTaskMutationSupport`'s `duplicate.goal = task.goal` all write the **task** record's own to-one. The `goal.habits` / `parent.subGoals` writes in `CadenceDeleteSurvivorSnapshot` are *undo* restorations that run only when a delete's commit is refused.
  **6. The evidence is a store test, not a source sweep.** `CadenceTrackingWriteRetirementTests` drives the real `PersistenceController.performStartupMaintenance` — not a replay of it — over a store seeded with one row of every shape a retired pass reacted to (a pursuit owning a parentless child goal and a goal-less child habit; a habit-day duplicated across two rows; a habit whose `reminderMinuteOfDay` is 1440; a goal list link), and asserts the four tracking tables come out with identical **row identities**, read back off a second `ModelContext` on the same container, plus the three field-level writes that no count could see. Identities and not counts on purpose: the retired passes mint on one table and delete on another, which leaves counts intact. `theFixtureHoldsEveryRowARetiredPassUsedToReactTo` is the control — every assertion here is satisfied by an empty store, so if the fixture stops holding one of those rows it goes red first. **It reads the real tree** (`theMCPWriteSurfaceAdvertisesNoGoalOrHabitConstructor` scans three source files), so the sweep manifest owes it a line.

  sitting, and nothing in the repo said so or guarded it.** Filed by `tzindep` 2026-09-08, out of the
  same red run as [[T-1115]]: nothing in the code changed, the machine's zone did. Three layers,
  because any one of them alone is wrong.
  **1. The run is now reproducible.** The scheme's `TestAction` had **no** `EnvironmentVariables`
  block and carried `shouldUseLaunchSchemeArgsEnv = "YES"`, so it inherited the Launch action's
  environment and pinned nothing. It now has its own block with `TZ=UTC` and stops inheriting.
  Deliberately **not** the LaunchAction, which would also have pinned the app a human runs from
  Xcode to UTC — a product-surface change made in service of the suite. Not inheriting costs the
  Launch action's `OS_ACTIVITY_MODE=disable` and its three CoreData logging arguments, so those are
  re-spelled in the TestAction and asserted.
  **2. Pinning alone would have HIDDEN the bug it came from.** A suite pinned to UTC can never catch
  "this breaks west of UTC". So the zone-sensitive shared date surfaces are exercised across an
  explicit set — UTC, `Asia/Tokyo` (positive, no DST), `America/Los_Angeles` (negative, with DST) —
  including both 2026 US transitions, where a day is 23 or 25 hours long.
  **3. Nothing re-acquires the dependency the pin now hides.** A sweep over this target's own
  `@Test` bodies fails on any test that derives a calendar day from the ambient zone instead of
  stating one. **The inclusion rule is a conjunction, and that is the point**: measured over 315
  files on 2026-09-08, the ambient needles alone appear in **50** tests across 14 files — most
  reading a `Calendar` only to add an hour to an event — while ambient **and** a day-boundary
  derivation is **22** across 11, which is the family T-1115 came out of. Bare `Date()` is the
  weaker, separate finding (a clock race, which the pin does not fix): 40 files hold one, so it is
  ledgered per file and may only shrink, rather than mass-rewritten.
  **Measured, not reasoned**: `TZ` in the environment does reach Foundation (`TZ=UTC` →
  `TimeZone.current` spelled **`GMT`**, so the assertions read the offset, not the identifier), and
  a *shell-level* `TZ=` does not reach the spawned test host — which is why the pin is asserted from
  inside a test rather than assumed. `WeekKeyResolutionTests` is the one exemption, by file: its
  subject **is** the parameterless helpers' device-zone default, so it cannot state a zone instead.

- [T-1115] **CLOSED 2026-09-09 (agent `weekkeytz`, landed by the coordinator) — `weekKey` reads the caller's time zone, so the pair round-trips at every longitude.** Originally filed as: `DateFormatters.weekKey(from:)` reads the *device's* time zone while
  `weekStartDate(forWeekKey:calendar:)` reads the *caller's*, so the pair only round-trips east of
  UTC.** Filed by `weekkeytz` 2026-09-08 at `8c45c91`, where a full `-only-testing:CadenceTests` run
  is RED — `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=65`, 400 issues, every one of them
  `WeekKeyResolutionTests.everyWeekKeyRoundTripsBackIntoItsOwnWeek`, and every one the same shape:
  `(DateFormatters.weekKey(from: monday) → "2025-W52") == (key → "2026-W01")`. Off by exactly one
  week, all 400 iterations. Two findings, and the second is the more expensive one.
  **1. The API asymmetry.** `weekStartDate(forWeekKey:calendar:)` sets `iso.timeZone =
  calendar.timeZone` — deliberate, and the whole point of `c424f42`. `weekKey(from:)` builds its own
  `Calendar(identifier: .iso8601)` two declarations above and **never sets a time zone**, so it
  silently takes the device's. Hand it the Monday-00:00-**UTC** that `weekStartDate` just returned
  for a UTC calendar and a Mac west of UTC calls that instant *Sunday*, i.e. the previous ISO week.
  Measured here by direct computation outside the test host, mirroring both helpers: 400/400
  mismatches under `America/Los_Angeles` and `America/New_York`, **0/400** under `Asia/Shanghai`,
  `Europe/London` (BST) and `Pacific/Auckland`.
  **2. The suite's greenness has been a property of the machine's location.** Nothing about the code
  changed between the green runs and this red one; the Mac's time zone did. `c424f42` was authored
  at `+0800`, where the round-trip is exact, so the test recorded the sum of a real API asymmetry and
  the author's longitude and reported it as a pass. A test that only passes east of UTC is an
  instrument blind to its own environment — it was never measuring the property it names. Note also
  that `TZ=…` does **not** reach the spawned macOS test host: `TZ=Asia/Shanghai` and
  `TZ=America/Los_Angeles` produce byte-identical 400-failure runs, so the zone cannot be varied
  from the outside and the correction has to be that both halves take a calendar.
  **Not a user-facing defect, verified rather than assumed.** `DateFormatters.ymd` pins a locale and
  no time zone, so `date(from:)` parses to *local* midnight; every shipping caller of the week
  helpers therefore stands in the device zone on both sides and agrees with itself. Enumerated at
  `8c45c91`: `NotesView.swift:262`, `CadenceNoteDateNavigation.weekRangeLabel`/`weekKey(forDayKey:)`,
  `CadenceNotesListSupport:356`, `CadenceMCPServiceSupport:40`, and `currentWeekKey()` — every one
  takes the `.current` default, and the two declarations that *do* accept a `calendar:`
  (`CadenceNoteDateNavigation.title`, `weekRangeLabel`) are never handed a non-current one outside
  the tests. **This matters because `weekKey` output is persisted** (`Note.weekKey`,
  `WeeklyNote.weekKey`) and syncs through CloudKit, in Production since 2026-09-05: no stored key may
  change meaning, so the fix must be default-preserving.
  **The fix:** give `weekKey` the courtesy `weekStartDate` already has —
  `weekKey(from:calendar: Calendar = .current)` setting `cal.timeZone = calendar.timeZone` — and have
  the test pass its `utc` calendar to both halves of the round-trip.

- [T-2085] **CLOSED 2026-10-06 (agent `runstate`) — both halves fixed, and the second one is fixed so that it cannot recur rather than by anybody remembering to check first.** The diagnosis in this entry is correct in every particular and I reproduced it deliberately before fixing it. **(1) THE BUDGET.** Root `AGENTS.md` is **199 lines by `wc -l` / 200 by the test's count**, against the 200 the test allows, and the byte count is 14004 of 18000. The eight-line triage bullet `1d8786cd` added is **one line** now — HEAD's own first line of it, kept verbatim, which is also what proves the reconstruction was rebuilt on HEAD rather than on the revision before it ([[T-1246]]'s escape from `REBUILD-BEHIND-HEAD`, taken instead of `--commits-stale`) — and its seven lines of detail moved to `docs/AGENTS_REFERENCE.md` under *"Telling a queued run from a wedged one (moved out of AGENTS.md, 2026-10-06)"*, which is the pattern [[T-1391]]/[[T-1392]] documents and which that file already carries five of. `lineBudget` was NOT raised. **Worth knowing: there is now ZERO headroom.** The file was 198 lines before `1d8786cd` and is 199 now, so the next line anybody adds to root `AGENTS.md` fails this test; the next addition there has to displace something, which is what the budget is for. **(2) THE RUNNER REWRITTEN UNDERNEATH ITSELF, REPRODUCED IN ISOLATION FIRST.** A four-line zsh script was truncated and rewritten with forty lines one second into its own `sleep`: it ran its own four lines and then executed **thirty-six lines that were never part of its program**. That is `zsh` reading a script incrementally by byte offset into one open fd, and it is exactly `xcb-widgetdrop-tests` re-running its whole test phase. **It happened a SECOND time, to this entry's own cause.** `1d8786cd`'s author appended ~60 lines to `scripts/xcb.sh` at 01:52 while their own verification run was in postflight; that run had already printed its complete `== xcb result ==` block and was found 40 minutes later executing `test-host-lock.sh acquire` **as a child of itself**, holding the test-host lock and queued behind it at the same time, with `uiseed` and `precheck` stuck behind that. Killed, the lease reclaimed on owner-death, and `uiseed` took the lock 16 seconds later. **THE FIX IS THE ONE THIS ENTRY SUGGESTED**, at the top of `scripts/xcb.sh`: the runner copies itself to `${TMPDIR}cadence-xcb-self.<pid>.<n>.zsh`, re-execs from the copy, and **unlinks the copy immediately** — the fd stays valid (probed), so there is no path left for anyone to edit and no litter either. `exec` keeps the pid, which is what the log name and the lock ticket are keyed on, and `SCRIPT_PATH`/`ROOT_DIR` are carried across explicitly so `$here` and `$ROOT_DIR/scripts/test-host-lock.sh` keep naming the real checkout. It **fails open**: a runner that will not start because it could not copy itself would be worse than one that can be edited underneath it. **PROVED BY INDUCING THE REAL FAILURE, WITH THE CONTROL THAT MAKES IT EVIDENCE.** `xcb.sh selftest` section 14 (6 checks; 209 → 215 total, all green) starts a real `xcb.sh <id> test` against stubs and, while it is inside xcodebuild, **truncates and rewrites its own script file in place** with ~900 KB of injected program — far longer than the script, so the read offset cannot land past EOF. Guarded: no injected text, exactly ONE `== xcb result` block, postflight reached, no snapshot left behind, and **no zsh diagnostic naming its own script**. The CONTROL is the same scenario with the guard switched off, and it really does corrupt — it printed `…/ctl/scripts/xcb.sh:21756: unmatched "`, the same shape as `widgetdrop`'s `./scripts/xcb.sh:3336: command not found: the`. Mutating the guard away kills the diagnostic check. **AND THE OTHER HALF OF THE LESSON, which this entry does not state and which every agent needs: HOW you write the file decides whether this can happen at all.** `open(path, "w")` and an in-place editor truncate the SAME inode, which is what hijacks a running shell; writing a temp file on the same filesystem and `mv`-ing it over the target is a rename, leaves the running process's inode untouched, and is atomic. Measured both ways in one probe: the in-place form made the running script execute 36 foreign lines, the rename form left it printing its own three. **Every edit to `scripts/xcb.sh` in this commit was installed by rename while `uiseed` was executing the old copy, and `uiseed` was unaffected.**

A parameter that is accepted and never drawn is how a deleted decoration grows back, and the freeze snapshot's copy was additionally a second copy of a list's colour with nothing left to keep it honest. **FIVE PINNING ASSERTIONS RE-POINTED, NONE WEAKENED OR DELETED.** `rowHeightIsTheOnlyFigureThatDiffersBySurface` rebuilds the struct from sixteen fields instead of nineteen and stays exhaustive because the compiler names every stored field; `theFiveDriftedFiguresLandedOnTheMacOSSpelling` keeps **five** assertions, with `listLabelFontSize` — the other half of the same 13-against-14 label fork — taking the dead `listColorBarHeight`'s slot, deliberately not dropping to four; `theMacOSMetricsEnumForwardsToTheSharedFigures` swaps that figure for `listLabelFontSize` and `listTrailingItemSpacing` so the enum stays pinned to the list-row half of the shared struct; and the two `expectCallSites` pins whose macOS subject died — `bothPlatformsHeadTheirCompletedGroupWithTheSharedTitle` (`completedSectionAccent`) and `bothPlatformsTintTheirTodayGroupsFromTheGroupItself` (`group.accent`) — are pinned at **0 on macOS and 1 on iOS**, where the zero is the assertion and iOS's one is what stops it passing because the symbol was deleted outright. **TWO NEW TESTS CARRY THE BITE THE FIGURES USED TO.** A figure pin could only fail when somebody *changed* a number: a reinstated bar would arrive with its own constants and pass every surviving assertion.
```sh
# DEFECTIVE AS WRITTEN -- do not copy. `eventMessage CONTAINS` matches /usr/bin/log's own
# invocation records, both counters rise together, and this reads outstanding=0 over a standing
# prompt. Use `./scripts/xcb.sh check-automation` (T-2070, corrected 2026-10-07 by `envguard`).
req=$(/usr/bin/log show --last 6h --predicate 'process == "testmanagerd" AND eventMessage CONTAINS "Writer daemon requires authentication"' | grep -c 'Writer daemon requires')
don=$(/usr/bin/log show --last 6h --predicate 'process == "testmanagerd" AND eventMessage CONTAINS "Finished enabling Automation Mode"' | grep -c 'Finished enabling')
outstanding=$((req - don))   # >0 means a prompt is standing and NO macOS test run can work
```

- [T-2059] **CLOSED 2026-10-04 (agent `scrollclaim`) — the tasks page stopped scrolling whenever a drag opened sideways, and no SwiftUI gesture priority could have fixed it: a `DragGesture` on a row cannot hand a touch back to the enclosing `ScrollView` once it has one.** The owner: *"when im on ios, scrolling in the tasks page sometimes doesnt work."* **Reproduced on `Cadence-iPhone15` before anything was changed**, by injecting two drags that differ in nothing but their first three samples. A 168pt drag straight up a task row scrolled the page 157pt. The same drag, from the same point, opening with **14pt of sideways travel** and then running the same 168pt up, scrolled the page **zero** — the screenshots are byte-identical but for the clock. That is the whole of "sometimes": whether the opening points of a thumb's arc happen to be straight. **The cause is this row's own gesture, proved by mutation, twice.** With `.highPriorityGesture(dragGesture, including: .none)` the failing path scrolled; with `including: .subviews` — which disables only the drag and leaves every descendant gesture alive, removing the confound in the first mutation — it scrolled again. **Three candidate fixes were refuted by their own builds, not by argument.** `minimumDistance: 30` stayed dead. `.simultaneousGesture` stayed dead. Claiming the drag *vertical* and returning early out of `onChanged` stayed dead — a drag opening `(4, -13)`, which the old code reads as vertical on its first event, still scrolled nothing. So the file's own comment was **wrong where it mattered**: "It does not contest the enclosing `ScrollView`/`List` pan — that is a separate arbitration" is false, the arbitration is not separate, and the row wins it for any touch whose opening movement is not dead vertical. **The fix is to stop asking SwiftUI to do the one thing it has no word for.** `iOSRowHorizontalPanRecognizer` is a `UIGestureRecognizer` that goes to `.failed` **while it is still `.possible`** when the drag is not horizontal: a recognizer that fails before it begins never asks the scroll view's pan to stand down, so a declined drag scrolls as if the row carried no gesture at all. The decision itself lives in `CadenceSwipeActionSupport.axisClaim`, outside `#if os(iOS)` and therefore pinned by the macOS-built test target, and it reads the axis at a new `CadenceSwipeActionMetrics.claimDistance` of **24pt rather than 12** — measured, not chosen: the reported drag reads *horizontal* at 12 and *vertical* by 24, and a deliberate swipe travels 76pt to open a single action, so waiting for 24 costs it nothing. **The four invariants were each re-measured on the built app, not argued:** vertical scrolling works from a row and from the completion circle; a swipe opens the tray, a tap on an open row closes it, and a 260pt swipe commits the full swipe; a tap on the circle completes, a tap on the row opens Edit Task, and a tap on the estimate chip still opens its popover; and a 163pt swipe begun **on the completion circle** completes nothing. **One regression was found and fixed inside this ticket, and it is the same shape as the bug this container was built to close.** With the recognizer merely added, an identical 260pt swipe committed from the row's text and was *ignored* from the "45m" estimate chip — which sits at the trailing edge, exactly where a right-to-left swipe starts. Letting the two recognize simultaneously fixed that and re-opened the old bug: the swipe opened the tray **and** the chip's popover. The delegate therefore makes the row's controls *wait* for this recognizer (`shouldBeRequiredToFailBy`) and exempts pans, so the scroll view is never made to wait; on a tap there is no movement, the recognizer fails at touch-up, and the control fires as it always did. **The `DragClaim` enum and the `claim` state are gone**, and with them the stale-claim hazard that motivated this investigation: there is no longer a latch to go stale, because the axis is decided per touch by a recognizer UIKit resets itself. **KNOWN, not fixed here:** a vertical drag *begun on the completion circle* scrolls, but measurably less far than the same drag begun on the row's text (≈14pt against ≈67pt for a 152pt finger travel, from downsampled screenshots, so treat the numbers as ordinal). It is an improvement on scrolling nothing, and the cause was not chased. **NOT verified:** iPad, `List`-hosted rows, VoiceOver, Dynamic Type, and real-finger behaviour on hardware — every measurement here is injected touch samples on one simulator, and a real touch stream is smoothed in ways an injected one is not, so the *frequency* the owner experiences may differ from the sharp boundary measured here even though the mechanism does not.

- [T-2050] **OPEN 2026-10-03 (filed by agent `ciattrib` while landing [[T-1993]]) — should an unattributed commit turn CI RED, or stay the notice it is today? The recommendation is KEEP IT A NOTICE, and spend the alarm on the reading where a red is deserved.** [[T-1993]] landed `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s `push-attribution` job as a notice: the script exits 1 honestly and the step swallows it. Making it a gate is deleting one `|| rc=$?`. The argument for leaving it alone, in the order that matters. **(1) The red would be false about the code.** `main` is linear, so the tip's tree contains the intermediate commit's bytes and any break is still caught. What a grouped push costs is which commit to blame, not coverage. A job that goes red over a tree that is fine is a different lie from the one T-1950 is about, not the same one fixed. **(2) It is not actionable when it fires.** By the time the step runs, the commits are on `main`. There is nothing the person reading the red can change in the tree to satisfy it; the only remedy is *push differently next time*. A gate nobody can satisfy by editing anything is a gate that gets switched off — the same argument `CI-SKIPPED` and `report`'s deliberate exit 0 are already built on. **(3) The remedy is upstream and behavioural.** T-1950 says so itself: push after each landing. If an alarm is wanted it belongs in the pusher's own loop — `scripts/agent-commit.sh` or the heartbeat, which can refuse BEFORE the group exists — not in the runner that learns about it afterwards. **(4) It would fire constantly today.** The two commits at `main`'s tip on 2026-10-03, `a59379f6..f068a5b9`, already read `UNATTRIBUTED -- 1 of 2`. A gate that is red most of the time teaches people to ignore the colour, and this repository has that failure recorded twice already. **(5) There IS a reading worth a red, and it is a different one.** A code commit that was never pushed at all, or a run cancelled and never replaced, is a COVERAGE failure rather than an attribution one — [[T-1640]]'s `NEVER-PUSHED` and `CANCELLED` over `report`. If the appetite for one more red exists, spend it there. **Decide and record the decision here either way;** the point of filing it is that the notice is a choice someone made with reasons, not the shape the work happened to stop in.

(3) The earlier store folders are a **separate** decision from the recovery one: they are outside the app's current container, `migrateLegacyStoreIfNeeded` still reads them, and deleting them would make the migration's own fallback unreachable. The row that shows all of them today carries `directory` and `onReveal` and nothing else, on purpose — whatever this ticket decides, the delete does not belong on that row. Note that `status` already prints the device as `free`, which is the same claim in the other direction. Until both land, the script's header and the script disagree, and the header is the half that is right.

That is the identical mistake to the bug itself, testing the documented intent instead of the allocation. Rewritten so the fixture lists a second fake **first**, standing in for the owner's device, via a `CADENCE_SIM_DENY_EXTRA` hook that is **additive only** — one that could remove an entry would be a way to hand out the owner's device by setting an environment variable. Both polarities asserted; re-mutated and **killed**, the failure naming the denied udid it wrongly allocated. Selftest 5 properties / 0 failures, live `claim` now answers `Cadence-iPhone15`. Thank you for filing it rather than working around it.

The queue property needed its fixture extended to hold the new fake too, or waiters got served instead of queueing and it reported *"queue has 0"*. Selftest is 5 properties, 0 failures.

Reproduced independently in arithmetic outside the test before being believed. So the figure T-1723 chose as a safeguard against *a corner painted over* is, at small picture sizes, the thing that refuses the product's own affordance — which is the opposite of what it was added for. **Why that is a defect and not a curiosity.** `MarkdownImageAssetService.minDisplayWidth` is 120pt (verified at `MarkdownImageAssetService.swift:159`), which at the fixture's 8:5 is 75pt of height — **half** the 148pt floor. `testTheBadgeAllowanceCannotHoldTheBadgeOnAPictureAtTheProductsMinimumWidth` asserts this against a control, which is the part that makes it evidence: the *same* badge on the 640×400 picture is clean and on the minimum-width picture is refused, so the difference is the picture's size and nothing else. The text case is held by the allowance's **shape**, not by its size, and the ticket's expectation conflated the two. `maximumFillOfTheAllowance: 0.7 → 1.0` turned the filled-corner case red as predicted. **One of the two remaining window-only questions is answerable from source after all, and the answer is that nothing else is drawn inside the picture's box.** `MarkdownEditorTextViewDecorations.swift` fills the rounded backing plate at `imageRect.insetBy(dx: -1, dy: -1)` (`:203`) and strokes the selection ring at `imageRect.insetBy(dx: -2, dy: -2)` with `lineWidth = 2` (`:220-223`) — a 2pt stroke centred 2pt out spans 1pt to 3pt **outside** `imageRect`, so neither is inside it — and the picture itself is drawn by `image.draw(in: imageRect, …)` (`:206`), an unclipped rect, so the image covers its own corners rather than letting the rounded plate show through them. (4) A vacuous iOS build must certify nothing, exactly as the macOS one does not ([[T-1147]]). It compiles only — no iOS tests run — so [[T-535]]'s hole is narrowed to the warning half and not closed. Reporting is the whole ask, and the honest severity is small: this is an instrument gap, not a coverage gap, and it should be filed in the report that way or it will be fixed twice.

- [T-1493] **OWNER-REPORTED: the month scroll puts the month TITLE between the weekday header and the grid that header labels, and renders the next month's title with no dates under it.** Filed 2026-09-28 after the owner looked at the same date popover the coordinator had screenshotted and called it *"this weird looking thing"* — which is the finding, because the coordinator had seen both halves and filed neither. **Structure, read from source.** `CadenceDatePicker.swift:139` draws the weekday symbols **once**, above the scroll; inside it, `LazyVStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 14)` emits one section per month, each beginning `Text(DateFormatters.monthYear.string(from: month))` and then its day grid. So the reader's eye goes **`Su Mo Tu We Th Fr Sa` → `August 2026` → `1`**, and the column labels are separated from the columns they label by a title. One header for a multi-month scroll is the right idea — repeating it per month would be worse — but the title must not sit between them: either the month title goes **above** the weekday header, or the header becomes a pinned section header per month. **The second half is the same `LazyVStack`:** `September 2026` renders as a heading with **nothing beneath it**, directly above the `Clear date` footer, because its grid is below the viewport. A month title with no dates under it reads as a rendering fault; cropping the section title with its grid, or clipping at a grid boundary rather than mid-section, is what removes it. **Why this was not filed last night, which is the part worth keeping.** The coordinator saw the header placement, noted it in [[T-1492]] as *"a judgement call deliberately left open"*, and reasoned that because it is identical on macOS and iOS it must be a pinned header rather than an accident. **Consistency is not correctness** — a structure wrong on both platforms is wrong twice, not deliberate. The orphan `September 2026` heading was not noticed at all. Both were obvious to the owner in one glance at the same image, which is the standing finding of [[T-1429]] arriving again: the instrument here was the coordinator's reading, and the correction came from someone looking. **Not implicated:** the seven-column grid itself, the selected-day marker and the continuous scroll all render correctly, and this is the DEFAULT text size — [[T-1440]]'s accessibility reflow is not involved. Pairs with [[T-1492]] (the quick pills above it); one visit to `CadenceDatePicker.swift` should take both.
  **CANCELLED 2026-09-28 — THE OWNER DECIDED both halves are fine and this ticket should not have been filed.** Shown the two findings, the answer was *"nah i actually think these 2 are fine"*: the shared weekday header above a multi-month scroll, and the next month's title appearing before its grid scrolls into view, are accepted as drawn. **The coordinator's FIRST reading was correct and was abandoned for a bad reason.** [[T-1492]] had already recorded the header placement as *"a judgement call deliberately left open"*, which was right; when the owner called the popover *"this weird looking thing"*, the coordinator read that as a verdict on everything in the frame rather than asking which part, reversed a sound judgement, and wrote a paragraph about consistency not being correctness to justify the reversal. The owner was reacting to the stacked pills — [[T-1492]], which STANDS and is unaffected by this cancellation. **The lesson is not 'trust the first reading'**, which would have been wrong for the two defects the same screenshots did find. It is that *"this looks weird"* names a feeling, not a boundary, and the cheap move — asking which part — was skipped in favour of inferring one. The entry below is kept rather than deleted because the reasoning is the record.

There is no two-row middle. **The arithmetic says the fallback is correct and the LAYOUT is still wrong.** On a 402pt iPhone the popover is about 305pt wide inside its 12pt horizontal padding; *Today* / *Tomorrow* / *This Weekend* plus two 6pt gaps come to roughly 295-300pt, so the single row genuinely does not fit — `ViewThatFits` is choosing correctly from what it was given. What it was given is the problem: **Today** and **Tomorrow** together are about 165pt and would sit on one row with *This Weekend* beneath, costing one extra row instead of two. - [T-1446] **CLOSED 2026-09-28 (agent `countcopy`) — one of the three is a defect and it is the first; the other two are correct as drawn and the arithmetic says so.** **(1) FIXED, and the diagnosis is a question asked one word wrong.** `CadenceEmptyStateCopy.isNarrowedToEmpty` took `filterNarrows`, which answers *is a narrowing filter selected* — true on both pages by default, and `everyDesktopFilterKnowsWhetherItHidesAnything` already pins that Goals opens on *Active* and Habits on *Due Today*. The question the copy needs is *is the filter hiding anything*, and on an empty store the two part company: nothing can be narrowed out of an empty collection. Defaulted to `true`, so the attach-lists sheet — whose `filterNarrows` is already a constant `false` — reads as it did. **(2) CORRECT AS DRAWN, measured.** Both halves the report names are the design, not an accident. `CalendarMonthGridMetrics.rowHeight` is `viewportHeight / weeksInMonth`, so a month block is **exactly one screen tall** and an empty week row is full height by construction; shrinking it would make the row pitch depend on content and break the offset table `CalendarMonthGridSupport.cumulativeOffsets` shares with the renderer, which is the one thing keeping the header from naming a month the grid is not showing. "Opens on the 6th" is `blockFirstDay(of:)`: a block begins on its month's first Sunday and the 0–6 days before it render as trailing fill on the block before, which is how the grid tiles months **without repeating a day** — Sep 1 2026 is a Tuesday, so September's block opens on the 6th. Clipping is possible only under the documented `minimumRowHeight` floor of 72 ("a very short window scrolls instead of shrinking rows into illegibility"), i.e. a grid viewport below `72 × weeks` — **288pt** for September's four rows, **432pt** for a six-row month. The app enforces `.frame(minWidth: 960, minHeight: 600)`, and the chrome above the grid is the calendar toolbar (12+12 padding over a 22pt title ≈ 52pt), two dividers and the weekday header (8+8 over 11pt ≈ 29pt) ≈ **83pt**, leaving **≥ 517pt**. **The block cannot overflow any window the app permits**, with 85pt to spare in the worst case. Nothing changed. The capture itself could not be re-taken: agent-launched macOS windows report `kCGWindowIsOnscreen = false` from this session, so this is read from source and arithmetic and says so. **(3) CORRECT AS DRAWN, and it is a control rather than a chip.** `KanbanCardView.emptyDueDateMetaItem` is drawn deliberately, gated on `task.shouldShowDueDateField`, and `metaChip` routes its `.dueDate` action to a `KanbanDateMetaButton` that opens the due-date picker — clicking the valueless `Due` chip is how you *set* a due date on a board card, and removing it would take the board's only route to that. The comment beside it already states the rule the filing re-derived: "An empty chip states nothing, which is why the shared descriptor does not produce it" — the shared `CadenceBoardCardMetadata` does not, and only macOS adds the affordance. **One nuance worth recording rather than fixing:** the Calendar Board passes `dayAlreadyStatedBySurface: dateKey`, which drops the do-date chip, so on that surface the row designed as a *date pair* degenerates to a lone valueless `Due`. It is still the picker; it just has nothing beside it to read as a pair with. The 4-of-7 day columns were not asserted either way in the filing and are not asserted here. **Gates:** macOS build `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=0`, 0 errors, **0 warnings**; full `-only-testing:CadenceTests` green. **Mutation-tested**: removing the `hasCandidates` guard and replacing `GoalsView`'s answer with a constant `true` each went red in the assertion named for it.

- [T-1487] **CLOSED 2026-09-28 (agent `uivalue`) — three fixes were weighed for a UI-level test and exactly ONE earns one, because only one of the three is pinned by a reading that cannot fail the way the owner's screenshot failed.** **The rule this run arrived at, and it is worth more than the test:** *a UI test earns its place here only when the defect is a property of the COMPOSED surface — a frame, a colour, a reachability — and the assertion that already exists is a proxy for that property rather than the property itself.* Three proxies are common in this repository and they rank differently. A **source scan** is the weakest: it asserts the code asks for the right thing, and it is green for every way the right request comes out wrong. A **model/simulator test** is strong where the thing measured is a value the model owns, and it is worth more than a UI test there, because a UI test cannot see model writes at all. A **pixel** reading is weakest of all and is already bounded by `CadenceUITestPixelSupport`. So the bar is not "is there a UI test for this" but "can the UI test fail on an input the existing assertion is green for", and the answer was yes once. **[[T-1432]] — YES, and the test is `CadenceUITests/CadenceTodayRowCrushUITests`.** Its existing pin, `CadenceTasksPanelMetricsTests.theRowsTitleIsLaidOutBeforeItsMetadata`, is a **source scan and says so in its own comment** — *"there is no seam that reports which subview won the width"*. It fails on exactly one event, a deleted modifier, and it is green for every layout those modifiers are present for: `.layoutPriority(1)` **orders** an `HStack`'s allocation and does not guarantee width, so a later `.frame(maxWidth:)`, a `.fixedSize` on a sibling, a padding that grows, or one more chip added outside the `ViewThatFits` all re-crush the title with every needle still in the file — and `.lineLimit(1)` is only one of the two reasons the due chip could come out three lines tall, the other being a width it cannot draw in, which no scan of that chip's body can see. The new test reads **four frames in points** off a window that really laid itself out, and **every figure is a comparison** rather than a threshold, because a width in points is not portable across a font, a display or an Xcode major and this project builds on two ([[T-1279]], [[T-1296]]): a new seed scenario `today-row-crush` plants **two Today rows with titles of the same length**, one carrying the screenshot's decoration (estimate chip, focus control, overdue due chip) and one carrying none, so the assertion is *the decorated row's title is more than half the width the SAME title got with nothing beside it* — about **0.1** in the owner's photograph. Three more readings come free and each fails on something the first cannot: the due chip's box measured **in title-lines** (a wrap is ~3, a correct chip is under 1); the decorated row's HEIGHT against the bare row's, which is the same fact from the row's side and is the only reading left if a row ever clips a wrapped chip instead of growing; and chip-past-the-row-edge / chip-over-the-title, which catch the fix's own failure mode in the other direction. Non-vacuity is asserted, not assumed: the decorated title must be **strictly narrower** than the bare one (or nothing is trailing it and the fixture has stopped crowding anything) and the bare title must be **narrower than its own row** (or the seeded title fits and there is no pressure to divide). **It clicks, drags and hovers nothing** — the app launches to `.today` — so unlike the two existing composed-window tests it is NOT behind the interactive opt-in and runs in every UI run. **[[T-1431]] — NO, and the reason is not cost.** What was fixed is a **count of model writes**, and XCUITest cannot observe a model write; the only thing it could observe is the value the roller lands on, which was never wrong. The existing pin is also not a source scan: `EstimateRollerMetricsTests` drives a **real `EstimateRollerCommitGate`** through a real live-scroll transcript and states the before number (11 writes) beside the after (1), which is strictly better evidence than a UI test could produce. The unmeasured half — *"it feels smooth"* — stays unmeasured, and a UI test would not have measured it either: `XCUIScreenshot` samples on demand, not per frame, which is the same reason [[T-1068]] leaves Today's flicker unpinned. **[[T-1433]] — NO, and this is the closest call**, because its pins are almost entirely source scans and a source scan cannot prove a surface is REACHABLE or that its fields are DRAWN. It still does not clear the bar: the realistic failure a scan misses here is content clipped out of a fixed popover, and the popover has no fixed height — `QuickCreateChoicePopover` frames `width` only and the form carries `minHeight`, so it grows to its content. Against that, a UI test would have to add product identifiers to an unidentified timeline canvas, synthesise the drag that opens the popover, and then assert *four rows exist* — which is the scan restated somewhere slower and flakier. Two things are recorded rather than done: a macOS popover is **its own `NSWindow`**, so `window.screenshot()` of the main window cannot see it at all and the pixel group is not merely expensive here but blind; and the one defect a UI test could uniquely catch in this area — a child picker popover occluding the composer that opened it — is **[[T-1480]]**'s, not this fix's, and it is expressible as GEOMETRY (two popover frames that overlap) rather than as pixels, which is worth knowing before anyone builds a fixture for it. **On [[T-1449]] and [[T-1480]] as a class:** a planted-fixture pixel invariant can catch a translucent fill (a known flat colour is no longer that colour) but it needs a saturated fixture inside the surface under test, and the only one that exists is an image in a note. Putting one inside a popover means test-only colour in product code; that is the line, and this run did not cross it. **No golden image was added and none should be.** **Verified:** scoped `CadenceTests` run over the five suites this change touches — `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=0`, **100** result lines, 0 failures, **0** warnings, **1068** swift compile tasks; and `build-for-testing` of the UI target, `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=0`, 0 errors, **0** warnings, with `CadenceTodayRowCrushUITests.swift` confirmed in the compile log so the count is not vacuous. **NOT VERIFIED, and it is the point of [[T-1488]]:** the new test has **never executed**. `scripts/xcb.sh` refused the UI run twice with *"the screen is locked"* — the [[T-563]] switch — and the brief's instruction was to report that and stop rather than retry in a loop.   **The scroll rule is one function with three rungs**, `CadenceScheduleSupport.initialTimelineHour`: the first timed item, else the current hour backed off an hour when today is on screen, else the work-hours start. Every item keeps one hour of context above it, the same lead "now" already had, because a block flush against a scroller's top edge reads as clipped. **(c) Re-entry: once per appearance, never again while the view lives.** `didPlaceInitialScroll` on iOS and `didRestoreTimelineScroll` on macOS are both `@State` one-shots and both stay that way — re-deriving on a scroll would move the canvas under a finger that was moving it the other way, and re-deriving on a data change would move it under a task the user had just dragged.
  **The two platforms do not share a scroll mechanism and were not made to.** iOS derives an offset and asserts it through a `ScrollPosition` once the canvas reports a content height; macOS restores a *persisted* `calendarRememberedTimelineHour` through a `ScrollViewProxy` id. So what is shared is the arithmetic, not the plumbing: `CalendarPageStateSupport.restoredTimelineHour` calls the same `initialTimelineHour`, and `bothPlatformsOpenTheSameDayAtTheSameHour` holds the two answers equal by construction rather than by two rules that currently agree — which is the drift [[T-596]] and [[T-1129]] are in the ledger for. **The first rung outranks macOS's remembered hour, and that has a real cost:** a user who scrolled to 14:00, left the page and came back now lands on the day's first block instead of at 14:00. It is the owner's sentence read literally, and the alternative keeps the complaint alive, since a remembered hour is written from wherever a scroll happened to stop rather than from a choice. Pinned in `theFirstTimedItemOutranksTheRememberedTimelineHour`, so reversing it is a decision and not a drift.
  **What was actually wrong was not the chip.** `showsToday` was read from `CadenceCalendarTimelineWindow.eventWindowDates` — a **28-day** EventKit *fetch* span, sized so its identity only changes once a week. Any week within a fortnight of today therefore answered "shows today" and opened at the current hour, and at 1 AM the current hour is the top of the canvas. That is the owner's week, and no amount of first-timed-item logic would have fixed it on a span with nothing on it. It asks `CadenceCalendarTimelineWindow.visibleDates` now — the columns actually on screen — and `theVisibleSpanIsTheColumnsOnScreenNotTheEventFetchWindow` states the difference.
  **Gates.** `CadenceTests` `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=65`, 0 compile errors, 0 anchored warnings, 4831 tests; the only two red suites belong to siblings in the shared checkout and not to this change — `CadenceCommentSymbolClaimTests` (comment claims left dangling by [[T-1273]]'s in-flight removal of `readyScheduleSlots` / `ReadyScheduleContext`, plus a renamed rollback pin) and `CadenceSectionEyebrowConvergenceTests` (`iOSTodaySchedulePanel.swift`, `todaypane`'s file). iOS Simulator gate `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=0`, 0 warnings, 1356 Swift compile tasks. Twelve new tests, all green, across `CalendarTimelineRangeTests` and `CalendarBehaviorRegressionTests`.

(3) *The selected destination being hidden* moves the selection to the **first visible row** (`CadenceSidebarLayout.selectionFallback`), both columns, on appear and on change — and the last visible nav row **cannot be hidden**, which the Settings screens say in a sentence rather than flipping the switch back.

The command palette reads the same resolved layout, so it cannot offer a page the sidebar is hiding.

The property is optional and read through `sidebarLayoutPreferenceRecords`; `anArchiveWrittenBeforeTheLayoutTableStillDecodes` deletes the key from a real encoded archive and imports what is left.

Focus keeps a Settings row whose drag moves nothing, which predates this ticket ([[T-1287]]). Schema wiring: `CadenceSchema`, `PrivacyDataResetService`, the export archive and the import plan, plus the four schema-driven coverage tables that make a missed one a failing test.

- [T-1182] **CLOSED 2026-09-20 (agent `mcpwrite2`) — a list and a context can now be *placed*, not just re-filed; the two display flags are readable and writable; and `linkedCalendarID` is refused with a reason rather than left unmentioned.** All four fields the ticket asked be decided together are decided. **No model change** — `Area.order`, `Project.order`, `Context.order` and the two `hide*IfEmpty` flags are all existing stored fields, so no CloudKit record type moved.

  **The ticket's premise is right and its implied fix is wrong, which is the part worth recording.** `update_container` leaving `order` alone on a move *is* correct and stays correct — both app editors do the same, and renumbering a list the caller only asked to re-file would be a third behaviour invented at this boundary. What was missing was an exit: `CadenceMCPOrdering.precedes` breaks an `order` tie on the **name**, so a list arriving in a context where a sibling already holds its number interleaves alphabetically. The obvious exit — accept a raw `order` and write it — **creates** that tie rather than resolving it, because the stored numbers are max-plus-one allocations with a gap wherever anything was deleted, so `[0, 2, 5]` is a normal bucket and a caller cannot name "third" by arithmetic. So `order` on both arms is a **zero-based position** among the rows the call leaves in the destination bucket, and the arm renumbers that whole bucket densely from zero. Dense is the point: it is the only state in which `precedes` never reaches its name leg, and it makes `CadenceContainerRef.order` read back as exactly the position that was asked for. A position outside `0...count` is refused naming the range, `columnOrder`'s rule for a partial order. The bucket the list *left* is not renumbered — the gap changes no sibling's relative position, and touching rows the caller did not name is the behaviour the paragraph above refuses. Areas and projects share one bucket per context and unfiled lists share their own (`nil == nil`), which is `nextListOrder`'s rule; contexts are one flat sequence, so `update_context`'s bucket is every context there is.

  **The undo covers the bucket, not the row.** A placement writes siblings no response of the call mentions, so the previous numbers of the *whole* bucket are captured beside `CadenceMCPContainerFieldSnapshot`'s field capture and both are put back on a refused commit; restoring only the named list would leave the bucket half-renumbered, which is the *visible* half on every surface that sorts on `order`. `aRefusedPlacementPutsEverySiblingsNumberBack` is the pin, and it is toolchain-neutral by construction ([[T-1296]]): a throwing `commit:` seam, never a `rollback()`. **The capture and the restore are written inside the two arms rather than in a snapshot type of their own, and that is a rule speaking, not a preference.** The first spelling put them in a `CadenceMCPRowOrderSnapshot.restore()`, and `CadenceSaveCommitDisciplineTests.noRenumberTheUserCanSeeSitsOverASwallowedOrMissingCommit` named the file: a declaration that renumbers `\.order` in a loop, owns its unit of work and reaches no commit is exactly what half 2b exists for, and a restore method reaches none. The half is right about the frame even where it cannot see the direction — the frame accountable for a rearrangement is the one that reaches the commit — so the loops moved into `updateContainer` and `updateContext`, where they are still fully visible to the sweep and still pass it. No exemption was added; that list is still `[:]`.

  **`linkedCalendarID` is refused, and that is a result.** T-390 (`Cadence/Models/AGENTS.md`) treats an `EKCalendar.calendarIdentifier` as opaque and permanent precisely so a dead link reads as unlinked rather than being re-matched by name. EventKit is in no MCP target, so this surface cannot enumerate the user's calendars: a caller could only echo an identifier it read elsewhere, and a wrong one binds a list to a stranger's calendar with no picker, no title in the response and `mcp-audit.log` for a record. A write whose result is invisible on this surface is the one shape this boundary refuses. The reasoning is on `CadenceUpdateContainerOptions`, not only here.

  **Inherited work, judged rather than adopted.** Agent `mcpwrite3` filed this ticket; agent `mcpwrite` began it and died on the session limit mid-change, leaving `order` on `CadenceContainerRef` and the two `hide*IfEmpty` flags on `CadenceContainerSummary` **with doc comments asserting that `update_container` wrote them, which it did not** — the intended end state documented as the current one, and `CadenceMCPToolContractTests.listToolDTOsDeclareTheirEstablishedStoredProperties` red because the DTO's field set is a contract and the spec had not moved with it. The read half is kept and is right; the claims are now true because the write half exists, and the `order` comment gained the sentence it was missing — the response carries the *stored* number while the argument takes a *position*, and the two agree only inside a bucket this arm has renumbered. The contract spec moved deliberately, with the reason on it.

  **Measured:** full `-only-testing:CadenceTests`, `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=0`, **4911 tests in 406 suites passed**, 0 compile errors, **0 compiler warnings** (0 `warning:` lines of any kind in the whole log, tool notices included), 346 swift compile tasks (non-vacuous). `CadenceMCPServer` built separately into private DerivedData: `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=0`, 0 errors, **0 warnings**, 465 compile tasks. Ten new `@Test`s in `CadenceWriteServiceTests` across this ticket and [[T-1122]], including the refused placement and the refused link insert. Two existing ledgers moved with the change rather than around it: `CadenceMCPToolContractTests.listToolDTOSpecs` for the DTO's new field, and `CadenceContextlessListSurfaceTests.knownContextDerivedListSites` 2 → 4 on this file, because `plannedListOrders` makes the `nil == nil` unfiled-bucket comparison twice more. `plugins/cadence-mcp/scripts/smoke-test.py` drives the placement over stdio — a board placed, the *displaced* sibling's new number read back off `list_containers` rather than assumed, the move reversed, and two refusals naming their range. `serverVersion` and `main.swift`'s handshake are both **0.10.0**: this is the first bump that changes a response as well as adding tools, additively. **Originally:** **Nothing on the MCP write surface moves a list, and `update_container` deliberately does not.** Filed 2026-09-12 by `mcpwrite3` while closing [[T-1120]]. `update_container` can re-file a list under a different context, and it leaves `order` exactly as it found it — matching `EditListSheet` and `iOSListEditorViews`, which both assign `context` on a move and renumber only on create. That agreement is right and it leaves a gap: `CadenceMCPOrdering.precedes` breaks an `order` tie on the **name**, so a list moved into a context where some sibling already holds its number interleaves alphabetically rather than landing anywhere the caller chose, and this surface has no way to say where it should go. Three stored fields are unreachable from the surface for the same "not in scope" reason and are worth deciding together: `order` (both lists and contexts — `create_context`/`create_container` set it once and nothing ever changes it), `linkedCalendarID` (T-390 treats the identifier as opaque; writing one from MCP means binding a user's calendar with no picker, which may well be the right refusal), and the `hideDueDateIfEmpty` / `hideSectionDueDateIfEmpty` pair (pure display preferences, cheap and harmless). Not urgent — nothing measured needs any of them — but "can this surface reorder?" is the first question a seeding job asks after "can it rename?", and the answer today is discoverable only by reading the schema.

- [T-1137] **CLOSED 2026-09-12 (agent `guardgate3`) — `default.profraw` is untracked, so nothing in the tree is tracked and ignored at the same time.**
  **Untracked, not un-ignored, and the choice is not a coin toss.** Two repairs close the
  contradiction: `git rm --cached default.profraw`, or drop `*.profraw` from `.gitignore`. The
  second makes every future coverage artefact a candidate for commit, which is worse than the
  defect it fixes. `.gitignore`'s own comment already classifies the file — *"Coverage/profiling
  artifacts left by xcodebuild runs"* — and the file answers to that description: `file(1)` reads
  it as *LLVM raw profile data, version 10*, mtime 2026-06-01, and its only two commits (`5e5e153`,
  `b5e4d36`) are broad refactors that were not about coverage. So the ignore rule is right and the
  tracking was the mistake. The file is left on disk, now ignored; only the index entry is removed.
  **Nothing reads it.** Checked across `*.sh`, `*.swift`, `*.py`, `*.yml`, `*.pbxproj` and `*.md`:
  every mention in the repository is *about* this defect — this ledger, `docs/AGENTS_REFERENCE.md`'s
  `rsync` history, and `scripts/agent-scratch.sh:63,184`. That was the confirmation the entry below
  asked for before anyone pulled the trigger.
  **This has happened before, which is a reason to expect it again rather than to relax.**
  `docs/TODO_DONE.md:2646` records an agent untracking *"a committed `default.profraw`"* already;
  it came back, because an ignored file is invisible to the human running `git status` and visible
  to any `git add <path>` that names it explicitly. Nothing here guards against a third round.
  **`agent-scratch.sh`'s workaround stays.** Its `git read-tree <base>` seeding is not reverted:
  it is correct for its own reason — a tree whose base is not HEAD needs it regardless of this file
  — and keeping it is what makes this closure checkable, since the 25-of-25 refusal it was written
  against can still be reproduced from any commit before this one.
  **The finding, as filed.** **`default.profraw` is tracked in git while `.gitignore` carries `*.profraw`, and the combination is invisible to `git add -A` against a fresh index.** A coverage artefact from some `xcodebuild` run is committed at the repository root. Being both tracked and ignored is not merely untidy: `git add -A` skips a path the ignore rules match unless the index already tracks it, so **any** tool that builds a fresh index over a tree — which is the natural way to compare a scratch copy against a commit — reads the file as deleted. Measured 2026-09-12 while building `scripts/agent-scratch.sh` ([[T-1094]]): 25 of 25 untouched trees were refused as holding uncommitted work, all 25 on this one file. Worked around there with `git read-tree <base>`; the file itself should almost certainly be `git rm --cached`'d, which needs someone to confirm nothing reads it.

The probe is a dotfile `sed -i ''` would have had to create, never the manifest, and the last expectation re-reads the committed bytes — if this host's write policy ever changes, the test goes red leaving a stray file, never a hole in the manifest. **The three mechanisms that are NOT the reason, each named so nobody reaches for the word "sandbox" again.** Exec of a setuid binary refused at `posix_spawn` — irrelevant, `/bin/zsh` is 755. - [T-1152] **CLOSED 2026-09-12 (agent `guardgate`, verified and landed by `guardgate3`) — a probe that cannot answer refuses, where it used to report a plausible zero.**
  **Two probes, one error, and zero was never the neutral answer.** `live_test_hosts` was
  `pgrep -f "$HOST_PATTERN" 2>/dev/null | wc -l`: stderr discarded, exit status swallowed by the
  pipe, empty stdin into `wc -l` printing `0` — the one value that unlocks the reclaim branch.
  `waiter_alive`'s `ps -o command=` had the same shape one level down, where an empty answer means
  *dead* and `prune_queue` acts on it for every ticket at once.
  **Told apart by two signals, not one.** stderr is merged into stdout and read, because pgrep's
  output is one pid per line and nothing else: exit 0 with all-pid lines counts; exit 1 with no
  output counts as a real zero (the ordinary idle box); exit >= 2 **or any non-pid line** is
  *cannot tell*, and refuses. The exit status alone would cover the sandbox measured today (3);
  the non-pid-line check is there because one observation of one OS is not a contract, and a
  future pgrep that complains and still exits 1 would slip back through a status-only reading into
  silent lock theft. `waiter_alive` gains a third return (2 = cannot tell) that falls through to
  the AGE check `prune_queue` already had, so nothing stalls and no live ticket is pruned.
  It returns through globals rather than stdout deliberately: `n=$(live_test_hosts)` runs the
  function in a subshell and would discard the reason string at exactly the call site that needs it.
  **Proven non-vacuous, failing-first, in the selftest itself.** `cannot-tell-refuses` builds a
  `pgrep` stand-in with the measured behaviour (says *"Cannot get process list"*, exits 3) over a
  fixture where a live host **does** exist, runs the OLD expression verbatim first and prints what
  it answered, then asserts the new refusal: *"the old reading answered '0'; this one refuses
  (rc=2) and the lock stayed with 'blindowner'"*. `cannot-tell-keeps-queue` does the same for `ps`
  over three live waiters: *"the old reading called all 3 waiters dead; a blind `ps` pruned none of
  3"*. Both run green at this commit, alongside the eight properties that predate them.
  **And in the real sandbox.** `CadenceTestHostSandboxCapabilityTests` now pins both halves of the
  measurement (pgrep exits **3**, not 1, and says something — a 1 with no output has to keep
  counting as a genuine zero) and runs `test-host-lock.sh status` from inside the host, asserting
  it prints `live test hosts: unknown` where it used to print `0`.
  **What this does not fix, and it is the larger half:** see [[T-1162]]. The refusal is correct and
  the pattern it defers to matches nothing.

There is no such caller today, and the fix is cheap: have `live_test_hosts` tell "no matches" from "could not ask" (`pgrep` exit 3 with output on stderr is not exit 1 with none) and refuse rather than reclaim when it cannot ask. - [T-1109] **CLOSED 2026-09-09 — an import is refused when it would leave a goal cycle with no root, rather than importing goals no screen can show.** From `docs/audits/2026-09-07/import-graph.md` (ROI-02); the finding was reasoned rather than measured, and the mechanism was confirmed against source before the fix.
  **Why no existing check caught it.** A resolvable `parentGoalID` is not an acyclic one. A goal that
  is its own parent, or a pair pointing at each other, satisfies every check already there: no id is
  repeated, every reference names a row that exists. What it produces is a component with **no root**,
  and the Goals page has no other way in — `GoalMissionGrouping.groups` starts at
  `GoalAssignmentRules.topLevelGoals`, which is `parentGoal == nil`. The goals import, sync to every
  device, and appear on no screen. `aRootlessGoalCycleIsInTheStoreAndOnNoGoalsRow` measures that
  consequence on its own, built by hand rather than through an import, so it stands if the guard moves.
  **The graph checked is the one the import leaves behind, not the archive's own edges.** A cycle can
  close through a row the archive never carries: overwrite one goal's parent edge and an untouched
  destination row on the other side completes it. So the map starts as the destination's and has this
  import's edges written over it, exactly as `upsert` and `wire` will write them.
  **A pre-existing cycle is not this import's to refuse.** Every goal has a single optional parent, so
  the graph is functional: each component holds at most one cycle and cycles are node-disjoint. "Is
  this cycle new" is therefore answerable *exactly* — it is new iff it contains an edge this import
  writes — rather than approximated by a depth limit, which answers a different question and would
  refuse valid archives. macOS deliberately *flattens* deeper descendants
  (`GoalMissionGrouping.nestedGoals`); it does not forbid them.
- [T-1110] **CLOSED 2026-09-09 — a refused tag attachment says what actually happened, instead of "Nothing was changed" over a tag that is on screen.** From `docs/audits/2026-09-07/recent-fix-claims.md` (ROI-05).
  **The mechanism.** `iOSTaskTagPickerPopover.addTag` is two commits, not one. The mint goes through
  `committedTag` and is durable the moment it returns — deliberately, since [[T-631]]: the moment the
  tag exists is the moment the user asked for it. Attaching it to the task is a *second* commit, and
  its refusal was reported with `CadencePendingChangePersistence.editFailureNotice`, whose second
  sentence is "Nothing was changed". On this path something was: the tag is in the catalogue, and the
  popover is still open over a live tag list, so the row is drawn directly above a notice denying it.
  **Both clauses of the replacement are true whichever branch `committedTag` took.** It returns
  non-`nil` only for a tag the store holds — one it minted and committed, or one that already existed
  — so "it's in your tag list" is not a guess about provenance. It deliberately does **not** say the
  tag was *created*: `committedTag` does not report that, and a sentence inferring it would be the
  same overclaim in the other direction. The second clause promises exactly what
  `iOSTaskTagStrip.commitTags(restoring:)` undoes, and nothing wider.

- [T-1114] **CLOSED 2026-09-11 (agent `focusimport`) — an import raises the cached focus totals of

  `rescue-import` 2026-09-07 from `docs/audits/2026-09-07/import-reconciliation.md` (ROI-04) — the
  fifth finding of that batch, and the only one `importgraph` did not reserve a number for before it

  audit directory, which is untracked.
  **The audit was right, and its line references were not — checked before fixing, as the entry
  asked.** Read at `4ad2178`, re-read at `a92b659`: the merge skip it cited at `:837` is at
  `:974-975`, and the session insert-and-wire at `:788` is at `:660` and `:923` — [[T-1111]]
  restructured `apply` in between, which is exactly why the entry told the next agent not to trust
  them. The three the audit hung the *rule* on had not moved at all: `AppTask.actualMinutes` at
  `:230` (it said `:229`), `CadenceFocusLedger.reconciledTotal` at `:737`, `reconcile(in:)` at
  `:767`, and its single production caller at `PersistenceController.swift:150`. The mechanism
  behind them is unchanged and the arithmetic witness reproduces through the real importer.
  **What it was.** `actualMinutes` / `loggedMinutes` are not fields, they are cached totals over
  `FocusSessionLog` rows — `FocusSessionLog`'s own note says so, and the ledger is the rule. An
  import is the one writer in the app that can add a subject's rows **without touching the
  subject**: merge keeps the matched task, inserts the sessions the destination lacks beside it, and
  leaves the counter at the number it held before those sessions existed. Destination task at 10
  with `(previousMinutes: 0, minutes: 10)`, archive adding `(previousMinutes: 10, minutes: 20)`,
  ends holding 10 while its own rows say 30. `bank` heals only the subject it writes to and the
  store-wide sweep runs only at launch, so the minutes were in the store, invisible, until the next
  launch — and an hours-mode `Goal` folding `actualMinutes` into its progress read the low number
  meanwhile. Area and Project `loggedMinutes` are the same shape and are fixed by the same line.
  **The fix is one call, in the transaction.** `CadenceArchiveImportService.reconcileFocusCounters`
  runs after `wire` and before the single `save()`, so the raise is part of the same commit as the
  rows that caused it: there is no window in which a committed store holds a counter that disagrees
  with its own rows, and no second commit to fail on its own. It sits below `importArchive` rather
  than beside it, so a caller reaching for `apply` directly gets it too.
  **Deliberately *not* [[T-1112]]'s post-commit seam, which is the decision the filing asked for.**
  That seam reconciles the OS's pending reminders — work outside the store, which must happen after
  the rows are durable and is injectable because a test host cannot observe it. This is inside the
  store and must happen before they are. Widening the seam would have made the fix a second write
  that only the two UI mounts perform.
  **`reconcile(rows:)` is new and `reconcile(in:)` now delegates to it.** The store-wide pass
  swallows a failed fetch and answers `false`, which is indistinguishable from "the counters were
  already right" — tolerable at startup, where the next launch tries again, and not tolerable inside
  an import whose commit is what the user is told succeeded. The importer has every row in hand
  already (`DestinationIndex` fetched the destination's before the first insert; the inserted ones
  were added to it as they were made), so it passes them and there is no second fetch to fail. The
  rule itself is untouched: `max(counter, min(previousMinutes) + Σ minutes)`, raise-only and
  idempotent, which is what makes it safe in **both** modes — overwrite writes the archive's scalar
  over the destination's, and that scalar can be older than sessions this device logged since.
  **The mode copy now admits it.** Merge said records you already have are "left exactly as they
  are" and overwrite said they are "replaced by the archive's copy"; both are false for this one
  number, in opposite directions. `CadenceArchiveImportPresentation.focusMinutesNote` is one
  sentence appended to both branches rather than a clause written twice.
  **A stale doc comment is corrected in passing**: `reconcile(in:)` still said its startup call
  "is not landed yet (`docs/TODO.md` T-742)" long after [[T-742]] landed it, and a sweep documented
  as unscheduled is one a second caller looks unnecessary beside.
  Pinned by six `@Test`s in `CadenceArchiveImportSurfaceTests` — the 10 → 30 witness read back
  through a **second** `ModelContext`, so it is the commit being asserted and not the object the
  importer happened to hold; three imports of the same archive still 30 with two session rows, since
  a restore is something people retry; the Area and Project variants; merge not lowering a counter a
  partial replica cannot account for; and the negative control, a store whose counters already agree
  and a task with no rows at all, both untouched — plus
  `bothModesSayThatLoggedFocusTimeFollowsItsSessionRecords` in `CadenceArchiveImportEntryPointTests`.
  **One of those six was wrong on its first run and the run is what said so**, which is worth
  recording because it is the only place the two modes genuinely differ here. It asserted that
  *neither* mode lowers a counter, and overwrite mode does: the destination's bare 100 with no rows
  behind it is replaced by the archive's 10, which is overwrite doing exactly what its copy says.
  The property that actually holds is **coherence** —
  `overwriteTakesTheArchivesScalarAndStillCoversTheSessionsOnlyThisDeviceHas` now gives the
  destination 90 minutes of session rows the archive never had, and the counter ends at 100 rather
  than at the archive's 10, so the number on screen is the total of the rows the store holds under
  either mode.
  Measured: `-only-testing:CadenceTests` green at 4745 tests in 398 suites,
  `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=0`, 0 failures, 0 compile errors, 0 warnings, with the edited files' own
  `SwiftCompile` lines in the log so the warning count is not vacuous; `Cadence`, `CadenceWidgets`
  and `CadenceMCPServer` all built clean, the last because `Models/` compiles into it on Swift 6.
  **Mutation-tested 4/4 killed, 0 survived, 0 inconclusive, 0 invalid**, over a baseline green at 68 tests in the two import suites. M1 deletes the `reconcileFocusCounters` call
  — the defect itself, restoring the un-reconciled cached scalar — and four tests name it, including
  the overwrite one. M2 lets the ledger lower as well as raise (`total >` becomes `total !=`), killed
  by `aMergeNeverLowersACounterToATotalThePresentRowsCannotAccountFor`. M3 moves the call above
  `wire`, so an inserted row still belongs to no subject and contributes to no counter: killed by
